Rescuers search rubble in Cali as Colombia’s strongest quake in decades hits Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 11/08/2026 - 8:53 GMT+2 Rescuers in Cali search rubble after Colombia’s strongest quake this century, which killed over 130 people, left hundreds injured and many missing. … More In Cali, Colombia's third‑most populous city after Bogotá and Medellín, residents and rescue workers picked their way through shattered concrete and twisted steel on Monday 10 August 2026, searching for survivors as ambulances crowded the streets around collapsed buildings. The footage shows people clearing rubble by hand and passing debris along human chains, while injured survivors are led away from the wreckage. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT A six-month-old baby and her mother were among those pulled from beneath a five-storey building, while patients were evacuated from a hospital after part of the structure collapsed. A 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia, killing at least 132 people and injuring 570, according to an evening update from the Colombian Association of Capital Cities, with the toll expected to rise. The US Geological Survey placed the epicentre near San Jose del Palmar in Choco province, 400 kilometres west of Bogota, at a depth of 107 kilometres. Pereira alone reported 60 deaths, and 86 buildings collapsed nationwide. Newly inaugurated President Abelardo de la Espriella declared a national disaster, with more than 1,600 buildings damaged. With at least 188 people still missing, Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder appealed to Bogotá and Medellín for urgent assistance. The quake was Colombia's strongest in the 21st century. Photograph: Julia Reinhart/Getty Images Business Washington Post ordered to reinstate opinion writer fired over Charlie Kirk posts Arbitrator determined the Post improperly fired Karen Attiah, a union-protected employee, over social media posts Jeremy Barr Mon 24 Aug 2026 20.51 EDT First published on Mon 24 Aug 2026 11.42 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An independent arbitrator has ordered the Washington Post to rehire the high-profile opinion columnist Karen Attiah, abruptly fired by the news organization last September over comments she made on social media about Charlie Kirk , the then recently killed conservative activist. On Monday, an arbitrator ruled that the Post had violated her rights as a union-protected employee and ordered the newspaper to reinstate her and compensate her for lost wages. “This decision confirms what we’ve said from the start: I was doing my job as an opinion journalist, and doing that job is not misconduct,” Attiah said in a statement. “After spending over a decade of my career at the Post as an editor and an opinion columnist focusing on race, gender and global human rights, I’m relieved to finally have that record set straight … I hope that this win sends a message to journalists and media institutions everywhere that freedom of expression is always worth fighting for.” A Post spokesperson said the company respects the arbitration process but declined to comment further. It’s unclear if the company plans to appeal the reinstatement ruling. Attiah was backed by the union that represents most Post employees, the Washington-Baltimore News Guild, and Democracy Defenders Fund, a legal advocacy group co-founded by Norm Eisen. In his own statement, Eisen called it a “thunderous win” for Attiah and “a landmark decision for every journalist who refuses to be silenced”. Washington Post’s opinion editor resigns after just one year in role Read more The Post had argued that Attiah was fired for cause after violating the company’s social media policy, which dictates that employees “must not harm the editorial integrity or journalistic reputation of The Post”. After Kirk was shot and killed on 10 September 2025, Attiah took to social media and wrote: “Refusing to tear my clothes and smear ashes on my face in performative mourning for a white man that espoused violence is … not the same as violence.” She also posted: “Part of what keeps America so violent is the insistence that people perform care, empty goodness and absolution for white men who espouse hatred and violence.” According to the arbitrator’s record of the case, Adam O’Neal , the Post’s opinion editor, had emailed the company’s head of human relations the following morning and said that Attiah’s posts were “beyond the pale- completely unacceptable for someone associated with Opinions”, calling for an urgent meeting. A few hours later, the Post’s top brass, including Will Lewis , then the publisher, met and decided that Attiah’s employment should be terminated because of her social media conduct. O’Neal also testified in the case that Attiah’s posts created security risks for the Post and its journalists. “People were at this intense moment of violence in America, and we didn’t know what was coming next,” he said in a hearing for the case. “And we’re walking into a building that says Washington Post on top of it, and here there’s a columnist at Washington Post on this account that’s making these horrific comments and that was of deep security concern beyond the professional – beyond the publication standards and our policies.” Attiah was emailed a copy of her termination letter – “for gross misconduct” – later that day on 11 September. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion The union representing Attiah charged that she had not engaged in any kind of misconduct, “let alone gross misconduct”, and that her professional mandate included expressing opinions. The arbitrator, Sarah Miller Espinosa, concluded that it was improper to punish Attiah on the basis of potential security threats to other Post employees. “In the Arbitrator’s view, the Post’s witnesses’ testimony seems to attempt to hold the Grievant accountable for the actions of bad actors who were posting threats against her and The Post on social media,” she wrote. “To imply that the Grievant’s posts were justifiable provocation for threatened criminal acts or that the Grievant’s employment may be terminated for just cause because bad actors threatened The Post is unsupportable.” Calling the Post’s termination of Attiah “absolutely disproportional”, she concluded: “The Post’s rushed decision to terminate the Grievant approximately four hours after O’Neal became aware of the Grievant’s posts … is not supported by good and sufficient cause.” Explore more on these topics Business Washington Post US press and publishing Newspapers Washington DC Charlie Kirk shooting US politics news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Business Economics Banking Money Markets Project Syndicate B2B Retail

https://en.antaranews.com/news/429688/bo.text: Home Current Issue Body of Polish tourist swept away at Bali beach found Body of Polish tourist swept away at Bali beach found September 3, 2026 14:23 GMT+700 Bali Basarnas during the search operation for Polish citizen in Tembles Beach, Jembrana, Denpasar on Thursday (September 3, 2026). ANTARA/HO-Basarnas Bali) Denpasar, Bali (ANTARA) - The Bali Search and Rescue Agency (Basarnas) found the body of a 44-year-old Polish citizen, Marcin Dawid, who was swept away by currents at Tembles Beach in Jembrana District, Bali. “We received information from our colleagues at Air Kuning Beach that a body had been found on the shore of Air Kuning Beach,” Coordinator of the Jembrana Search and Rescue (SAR) Post Dewa Hendri Gunawan said in a statement on Thursday. The victim’s body was found by local residents at around 5:20 p.m. local time on Wednesday (September 2). According to Gunawan, the body was found approximately 7.5 kilometers west of the location where the incident occurred. Witnesses then reported the discovery to the local police, he added. SAR officers who received the report immediately went to the location to recover the victim’s body. “The victim was then taken to Negara Hospital by ambulance from the Jembrana Police Medical Unit for further examination,” Gunawan said. He explained that the search for the Polish national began after the victim arrived at Tembles Beach on Sunday (August 30) at around 6:00 p.m. Suspicions that he had been swept away emerged after his motorcycle and several personal belongings were found abandoned on the beach. The Bali Basarnas office received the report on Monday (August 31) at 5:55 a.m., initially identifying the victim as a British citizen. The victim was later confirmed to be a Polish national on the second day of the search after officers found his identity card. The three-day SAR operation involved searches by sea, land, and air. The team used a rubber boat to search the waters to the west and a thermal drone to conduct an aerial search. After initially yielding no results, the search concluded successfully on the third day after a resident reported finding the victim’s body. Gunawan said Basarnas was joined in the operation by the Jembrana Police, Mendoyo Sector Police, Indonesian Navy Pengambengan Post, Bali Regional Police Mobile Brigade Unit, Jembrana Indonesian Red Cross (PMI), Arjuna Rescue, and local residents. https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: ‘The reality of reopening the most divisive debate of recent British history will be drawn out, obstacle-strewn and fraught with political risk.’ Photograph: AFP/Getty View image in fullscreen ‘The reality of reopening the most divisive debate of recent British history will be drawn out, obstacle-strewn and fraught with political risk.’ Photograph: AFP/Getty Opinion Brexit The Guardian view on Burnham’s Brexit reset: an overdue show of ambition Editorial The prime minister is correct to judge the time is right to push for closer links with the EU. The political risk is far outweighed by the potential rewards Tue 13 Oct 2026 13.30 EDT Last modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 13.40 EDT Share T he German philosopher GWF Hegel famously evoked the owl of Minerva when discussing the historical wisdom that comes through hindsight. This autumn, she has flown tirelessly over the landscape of British politics. Party conference season was dominated by conflicting Labour and Conservative accounts of the 1970s and 80s. And a decade after the United Kingdom voted to leave the European Union, Andy Burnham this week abandoned all equivocation over the damage – economic but also strategic – that resulted from that decision. Having declared that it is time to “face up to the reality that Brexit has done more harm than good”, Mr Burnham told the House of Commons on Monday that it would be a “dereliction of duty” not to explore all options for closer relations with Brussels. Though he confirmed that in this parliament he will honour the red lines in Sir Keir Starmer’s Labour manifesto, all bets will subsequently be off. A long-delayed reset summit, Mr Burnham also announced, will take place next month with deals on food and drink and youth mobility to be negotiated. The former Labour leader Neil Kinnock asserted to an Italian newspaper on Tuesday that the prime minister’s “obvious” eventual objective was to rejoin. View image in fullscreen Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel (1770-1831). Photograph: Prisma Archivo/Alamy That might well be contested in Downing Street. But as has become the norm in this overture phase of Mr Burnham’s premiership, his Commons statement was bracingly expansive and forthright. It also had the signal virtue of being correct in its diagnosis and prescription. Nevertheless, the reality of reopening the most divisive debate of recent British history will be drawn out, obstacle-strewn and fraught with political risk. Labour’s hyper-caution over revisiting the EU relationship has increasingly been at odds with polls indicating a substantial majority of the public supports closer ties. But the devil will be in the detail. In the red wall, in particular, much will depend on the prime minister’s undoubted persuasive powers. The need to undo the economic self-harm of Brexit was not something that Mr Burnham chose to emphasise while campaigning for his seat in the leave-voting constituency of Makerfield. For its part, the EU itself is in flux and may have new red lines of its own. Responding to a more menacing geopolitical environment, Brussels is contemplating deeper coordination in areas such as defence and economic policy. The direction of travel is already evident in the “Made in Europe” strategy, which threatens to leave British-based car manufacturers out in the cold. As that risk illustrates, it is overwhelmingly in Britain’s interests to be acting in concert with the EU, rather than flailing in sorry isolation on the sidelines. Following the visceral mutual distrust of the Tory Brexit years, Sir Keir restored a basic if circumscribed civility to relations between the UK and the EU. Mr Burnham’s boldness can now open up new possibilities down the line for “a real reset”, to use the formulation of one EU diplomat. It will not have escaped Mr Burnham’s notice that such a prospect would unite progressive Britain behind it, and could significantly boost Labour’s percentage vote share. His overriding early theme has been the need to rectify the political “wrong turns” of past decades. Beginning the long task of doing so on Brexit is brave, but it promises significant dividends for his premiership and, much more importantly, the country. Poland: Kraków mourns six victims as shooting site reopens Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 8 November 2026 - 23:06 GMT+1 Kraków's historic main square in southern Poland reopened to the public on Sunday 8 November, just over 24 hours after a deadly shooting left six people dead and 15 others injured. Residents are lighting candles in memory of the victims, while bullet marks remain visible on café windows. … More Residents and visitors returned to the scene of the attack, where bullet marks were still visible on café windows and candles were being lit in memory of those killed. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Footage shows people stopping to examine the damaged glass, while others quietly pay their respects at a makeshift memorial on the edge of the square. One visibly emotional woman is comforted by a man as mourners gather around the candles. Police officers continued to patrol the area as pedestrians and café customers gradually returned to the normally bustling square. The attack took place on Saturday 7 November , when a 24-year-old gunman opened fire in the historic centre of Poland's second-largest city. The shooting triggered scenes of panic, with witnesses filming people running for cover as emergency services rushed to the area.
